index.meta.title: Can Rumi work in isiZulu, isiXhosa and Sesotho?
index.meta.subtitle: Rumi in South African languages · Sepedi, Afrikaans and Setswana also tested
index.meta.dateline: Measured 7 to 13 October 2026 · every number is labelled measured, proxy, AI-judged or native ear

index.answer.heading: The answer
index.answer.lead: Yes, with three conditions. Automated tests in all three languages show Rumi planning lessons, transcribing classrooms, drafting coaching and replying in voice notes; the first native listeners found its voice understandable, not yet natural.
bullets: Lesson plans and coaching are strong in all three languages; listening is the capability that separates them.

Speaking is intelligible to a machine; where first-language listeners have heard it (isiZulu), it is not yet natural: the first native listeners heard pitch in the wrong places and sentence openings that start wrong, and lost the meaning of one line. Afrikaans was the one voice a listener on that call praised (a listener who speaks Afrikaans). The other voices have not been heard yet.
Six languages, four capabilities, about a hundred dollars of metered model and voice calls.
index.answer.table_note: Scores are out of 10 and never round up. Click any cell to go to its evidence.
index.answer.native_ear: Native ear: the first native listeners heard the isiZulu voice on 9 October (understandable, not yet natural); no other output on this site has been checked by a first-language speaker yet.

index.method.heading: How we tested
index.method.lead: Two pipelines, six languages, English as the control; every score compares Rumi's output with a known-good reference by script.
bullets: Curriculum page to lesson plan: a vision model reads the official CAPS pages and the Department's Grade 1 workbook [[fn:fn-caps-zu]] [[fn:fn-wb-zu]]; a planner cuts Term 1 into fifty traceable days; a writer drafts and voices each lesson in the structured format partners use [[fn:fn-rti]].

Classroom recording to coaching report: the best transcription engine writes the transcript; the coaching engine reads it against the partners' coaching course [[fn:fn-coaching-course]], quotes a timed moment for every step it credits, and drafts the debrief.

References: the official file's own text, human transcripts of read speech [[fn:fn-fleurs]] [[fn:fn-nchlt]], the lesson transcript, and the spoken script. The three labels are explained below the diagrams.
index.method.samples: Feasibility-sized samples, not a benchmark: 19 lesson plans and 6 two-week overviews; 143 curriculum, workbook and reader pages; 32 to 70 read sentences per language; 48 recordings on the review page (33 partner, 15 public), with coaching reports on 14 partner classroom recordings; 6 spoken sentences per voice, and five sentences per language in the speaking review.
index.method.limits: Listening scores come from read speech in quiet rooms, an upper bound for a Grade 1 classroom. The World Bank structure check [[fn:fn-wb-tool]] tests structure our template enforces, so it sits beside the lesson-plan score, not in it.
diagram_lp: Vision reading, checked letter by letter against the official file
Term plan: 50 days traced to the curriculum
diagram_coach: Best transcription engine, second engine as a check
Steps seen / partly / not observed, each with a timed quote
Debrief: questions, five-step plan, next step
index.method.review_line: Two review pages, open to anyone who speaks the language: the [Listening review](review.html) plays the partners' own recordings beside what Rumi heard, line by line; the [Speaking review](speak.html) plays the same five sentences in five or six voices, blind, and asks which sounds like a first-language speaker. Those ratings become the first native-ear scores.

index.languages.heading: The three languages
index.languages.lead: Each page shows a lesson plan, one of the partner's own classroom recordings being transcribed, the coach's report on that recording, and a conversation with Rumi speaking.

index.also_tested.heading: Also tested
index.also_tested.lead: Sepedi, Afrikaans and Setswana ran the same tests without a page of their own; coaching was not run for Afrikaans and Setswana (no classroom recording sourced).

lines.nso: Sepedi (Funda Wande's Limpopo language; not Sesotho): coaching was run on one public reading lesson [[fn:fn-video-nso]]. The transcription engines disagree most here (19.0% to 36.6% of classroom characters on two public lessons [[fn:fn-video-nso-2]], proxy: two engines compared), so the agreement gate matters most. Its voice has not been heard by a first-language speaker; the isiZulu findings apply until the [speaking review](speak.html?lang=nso) says otherwise.
lines.af: Afrikaans: the strongest listening of the six; its voice, Paul Steyn, is a first-language Afrikaans voice from the ElevenLabs library, and the one voice a listener on the 9 October call praised (a listener who speaks Afrikaans). It has not been rated yet: [rate the Afrikaans voices →](speak.html?lang=af).
lines.tn: Setswana: the winning engine is fragile on longer audio, so the runner-up is the safer choice; the voice is designed to sound like a first-language Setswana speaker and has not been heard by one yet: [rate the Setswana voices →](speak.html?lang=tn).

index.also_tested.note: Sesotho and Setswana listening is scored on short read phone prompts with their own South African English control [[fn:fn-nchlt]], not the sentence set used for the other four [[fn:fn-fleurs]]; the two are not comparable.

index.scheme.heading: Scheme of studies for one book
index.scheme.lead: One Department of Basic Education workbook, turned into a week-by-week scheme that traces every lesson to its curriculum requirement; the sheet is open to anyone.
bullets: The six CAPS Home Language editions are one document in six languages (same sections, same Term 1 tables, same time tables); one configuration per language turned all six into requirement lists.
Book 1: 142 pages, 64 worksheets, four a week, eight workbook weeks a term; CAPS has ten, so weeks 9 and 10 carry no workbook pages. Arithmetic slips in the official PDFs are flagged, not inherited.
The workbook's order of new sounds differs from our CAPS-first plan (isiZulu workbook a, i, e, o, m, u…; our days a, e, i, o, u, m…); the sheet shows both, so the gap is visible.

index.ship.heading: What it would take to ship
index.ship.lead: The infrastructure work is small and known; the expensive part is one first-language reviewer per language for about an hour.
rows: Use the engine that scored best for each language for transcription, with a two-engine agreement gate so a transcription slip can never become a coaching question
Review the flagged lesson phrases (about seventy across six languages) and one transcript; rate the voices on the speaking review
one Foundation Phase teacher or coach per language, about an hour
Let native ratings pick the voice and the intonation settings per language, then record one consented three-minute clip per language so Rumi speaks in a South African coach's own voice
Share classroom recordings, lesson plans and the coaching course's field observation tool
Keep the back-translation check in the lesson pipeline; it caught errors the structure checklist cannot see
Make every pilot teacher a rater: one sentence of Rumi's voice, then natural, understandable or lost, and a "say it right" reply

index.partners.heading: What the partners can give us
index.partners.lead: Five things, in order of how much each moves the numbers.
bullets: Native ears on the voice: ten minutes per language on the speaking review, from a teacher or coach who speaks it at home; the Sesotho and Sepedi reviewers named on the call most of all.
Native ears on the transcripts: an hour per language on the listening review.

Raw, phone-recorded classroom audio, the way a teacher would actually record it: Funda Wande's raw isiXhosa footage, VVOB's KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumalanga footage. Every recording so far was produced with a microphone on the teacher.
A coach's voice: one consented three-minute recording per language, once native ratings have picked the engine.
The coaching course as used in the field: its observation tool, the teacher reflection instrument, and term plans or pacing guides per grade.

index.cost.heading: What this cost
index.cost.lead: About a hundred dollars of metered model and voice calls for six languages, four capabilities, 19 lesson plans, 12 classroom recordings and about 300 speech tests; authoring and judging ran on subscription seats.
index.cost.note: Read from our spend ledger on 13 October 2026, including the listening review (48 recordings transcribed and checked), the voice auditions and the interactive demos on this site.

index.sources.heading: Sources
index.sources.lead: Every document, recording and dataset used, linked to the exact file. The partners' own recordings play on the Listening review page; their coaching course is credited but not public.

index.footer.line: Built by Rumi. Lesson plans, transcripts, reports and voices on this site are Rumi drafts. The first native listeners have heard the isiZulu voice; nothing else has been checked by a first-language speaker yet.

verdict.heading: isiZulu at a glance
verdict.native_ear: Native ear: two first-language isiZulu speakers from the coalition heard Rumi's voice on 9 October and found it understandable, not yet natural; one read two of the lesson plans and called the pedagogy sound. No line on this page has been checked word by word yet.
verdict.lead: GREEN on all four automated tests, and the language the first native listeners heard: the voice is understandable, not yet natural. Listening and coaching below run on VVOB's own classroom recording, Module 6 · Phonics · Lesson 6 · Checking sounds; coaching was also measured on three VVOB training videos.
verdict.material: Material: CAPS [[fn:fn-caps-zu]], the Grade 1 workbook [[fn:fn-wb-zu]], three readers [[fn:fn-asb-zu]], a speech set [[fn:fn-fleurs]], VVOB's classroom and training recordings [[fn:fn-vvob-videos]]; two public lessons in the first round [[fn:fn-video-zu]] [[fn:fn-video-zu-2]].

lesson_plans.heading: Lesson plans
lesson_plans.lead: Score 9.2: Rumi reads the official pages faithfully, cuts Term 1 into traceable days and writes real isiZulu.
bullets: Page misses are printer stamps and tracing rows, not words; five curriculum items are taught but paraphrased.
The only language below the real-word cap: the unattested words (namuhla, ikhanda, amahlombe) are everyday words the sources never use.
Fourteen uncertain phrases await a first-language coach.
lesson_plans.note: Beside the score: World Bank structure check 9.7 (AI-judged, two graders, three lessons) [[fn:fn-wb-tool]]. Only back-translation found "first bear" where "first sound" was meant.

listening.heading: Listening
listening.names_note: Names in the recording become [learner], [teacher] and [school]. Remarks to camera are labelled "Teacher (interview)" and are not coached.
listening.score_line: Gemini 2.5 Pro on 32 read sentences with human transcripts: 5.8% of characters wrong; English from the same set 1.6%.
listening.agreement_line: On this recording (VVOB, Module 6 · Phonics · Lesson 6 · Checking sounds) the two best engines agree on 91.7% of characters and disagree on 8.3%. No written isiZulu transcript exists for it, so this is a proxy, not an accuracy score; 6 lines the engine heard in silence were removed.
listening.lead: Score 8.8: the best engine gets 5.8% of characters wrong on read isiZulu.
bullets: The runner-up is under two points behind; a second set of short phone prompts agrees [[fn:fn-nchlt]]. On VVOB's recordings the engines disagree mostly on names, chants and songs.
A two-engine agreement gate stops a misheard name becoming a coaching question, as once happened in an earlier run.
listening.review_line: Help us check: [review the isiZulu recordings →](review.html?lang=zu) and mark each line right or wrong. No first-language speaker has done this yet.
listening.partner_line: On 19 of VVOB's 25 isiZulu recordings (48 of 79 minutes) the two engines agree on 91.0% of characters, and on the classroom lessons alone 88.1% (proxy: two engines compared, not checked against a person). That is the small gap from read speech we expect in a classroom. No written isiZulu transcript exists for these recordings, so their only measured accuracy will come from reviewers' corrections.

coaching.heading: Coaching
coaching.not_graded: The teacher is never graded: steps seen, partly seen or not observed, each with a timed quote, and one next step.
coaching.accuracy_note: These measure Rumi, not the teacher: quotes found, items filled, and whether three readings saw the same thing. Readings are compared with each other, not yet checked by a coach.
coaching.lead: Score 9.4, measured on VVOB's own classroom recording, Module 6 · Phonics · Lesson 6 · Checking sounds: 22 of 22 of Rumi's quotes found word for word in a classroom turn, 17 of 17 report items filled, and the three readings agreed on what they saw in 10 of 10 items. Measures Rumi, not the teacher; readings compared with each other, not yet checked by a coach.
bullets: The report below is on the recording that plays above; every timestamp seeks it. On two other VVOB lessons, Module 10 · Group guided reading and Module 13 · Lesson 5, part B, the three readings did not even agree on what kind of lesson they were watching; the score now moves when readings disagree.

The score rose from the first round because the reader changed (three independent readings that check their own quotes, where the first round used one lighter model) and the material changed (produced partner films, a microphone on the teacher); it does not mean Rumi got better.
AI-judged, beside the score and from the first round: feedback prose 5.0 out of 10 (understandable, not natural).
coaching.debrief_note: The debrief is read by the same voice as the conversation below, so the first native listeners' findings apply to it too: understandable, not yet natural.

speaking.heading: Speaking
speaking.chat_note: The teacher types; Rumi answers in voice notes. Rumi's lines were drafted and checked by two AI models; the words still need a native ear, and the voice has had its first one.
speaking.score_line: ElevenLabs eleven_v4, voice Neo: 0.2% of characters lost on the text-to-speech-to-text round trip (6 sentences, measured). That is intelligibility to a machine, not naturalness. An AI listener had rated this voice as native-sounding; the first native listeners showed that rating to be wrong, so no AI-judged nativeness number appears on this site any more.
speaking.lead: Score 9.9 measures one thing: a machine recovers the words (0.2% lost on the round trip). Two first-language isiZulu speakers from the coalition listened on 9 October and found the voice understandable, not yet natural.
speaking.note: What we are doing about it: a blind speaking review in which five or six voices read the same five sentences and first-language listeners rate each one, with intonation-tuned variants of the best voice among them; native ratings, not a machine, decide which voice ships. The earlier auditions below are kept for the record; their AI-judged scores are not.
speaking.listeners_line: What they heard: pitch rising where isiZulu does not rise; sentence openings that start differently from how a person speaks; the greeting Sawubona pitched as no speaker would pitch it; one line whose meaning was lost in the rise and fall; and more English words than a teacher would use. The written text, they said, is correct. On the same call, the Afrikaans voice was the one a listener praised.
speaking.review_line: Help us choose: [rate the isiZulu voices →](speak.html?lang=zu). The same five sentences in five or six voices, blind; about ten minutes.
speaking.trials_heading: Earlier auditions, reading the same sentence (round-trip loss only)

ship.heading: What it would take to ship isiZulu
bullets: Use the best-scoring transcription engine with the agreement gate; an hour from a first-language coach (fourteen phrases, one transcript) and ten minutes on the speaking review; then a three-minute recording for an isiZulu voice, in the engine and settings native ratings pick.

coaching.debrief_note: The debrief is read by the same voice as the conversation below, so the first native listeners' findings apply to it too: understandable, not yet natural.

speaking.heading: Speaking
speaking.chat_note: The teacher types; Rumi answers in voice notes. Rumi's lines were drafted and checked by two AI models; the words still need a native ear, and the voice has had its first one.
speaking.score_line: ElevenLabs eleven_v4, a voice made with ElevenLabs Voice Design from a written description of a first-language Sesotho speaker: 1.1% of characters lost on the text-to-speech-to-text round trip (6 sentences, measured). That is intelligibility to a machine, not naturalness. An AI listener had rated this voice as native-sounding; the first native listeners showed that rating to be wrong, so no AI-judged nativeness number appears on this site any more.
speaking.lead: Score 9.7 measures one thing: a machine recovers the words (1.1% lost on the round trip). No first-language Sesotho speaker has heard this voice yet.
speaking.note: A designed voice is generated from a description, not cloned from a person. What we are doing about it: a blind speaking review in which five or six voices read the same five sentences and first-language listeners rate each one, with intonation-tuned variants of the best voice among them; native ratings, not a machine, decide which voice ships. The earlier auditions below are kept for the record; their AI-judged scores are not.
speaking.listeners_line: The isiZulu voice from the same engine was heard by two first-language speakers on 9 October: understandable, not yet natural, with the pitch wrong at sentence openings and the meaning of one line lost. We assume the same of this voice until the speaking review says otherwise.
speaking.review_line: Help us choose: [rate the Sesotho voices →](speak.html?lang=st). The same five sentences in five or six voices, blind; about ten minutes.
speaking.trials_heading: Earlier auditions, reading the same sentence (round-trip loss only)

ship.heading: What it would take to ship Sesotho
bullets: Funda Wande's remaining recordings and lesson plans, a Sesotho mapping of the observation instrument, the Sesotho reviewer named on the call for the twelve phrases, the transcripts and the voice, the agreement gate, and a Sesotho voice from a coach's recording once native ratings pick the engine.

steps: Pick your language, then open a recording. The transcript follows the audio line by line.
For each line, tap Right, Wrong or Not sure. If it is wrong, type what was actually said.

scores.heading: What the score labels mean on this page
scores.measured: Measured: Rumi's transcript was compared, character by character, with a reference in the same language: the recording's own captions, a published transcript, or the corrections reviewers have typed here.
scores.proxy: Proxy: two engines compared; not checked against a person. No reference exists, so two transcription engines were compared with each other. Where they disagree, at least one is wrong; where they agree, both can still be wrong.
scores.ai_judged: AI-judged: a model scored this number. Here that is the meaning check: how much of the meaning Rumi recovered, against the partner's own English subtitles. It measures listening and translation together, and a model's judgement is not a person's.
scores.pending: Native ear pending: no first-language speaker has checked this recording yet. Your checks change that.
scores.partner_reference: The partners' recordings have no written transcript in the language spoken, so nothing can be measured against them yet. On these recordings the only measured accuracy will come from reviewers' corrections on this page.
scores.read_sentence: A read sentence is a few seconds of speech scored against its published transcript. It shows what measured looks like; it is not a language score.
scores.meaning: Meaning recovered: how much of the meaning Rumi recovered, against the partner's own English subtitles. AI-judged.
scores.removed_in_silence: {n} lines the engine heard in silence were removed.
scores.removed_in_silence_one: 1 line the engine heard in silence was removed.
scores.reviewer_label: {pct} of characters wrong, from {n} reviewer corrections

partner_notes.zu: On VVOB's isiZulu recordings the two engines agree on 91.0% of characters, 88.1% on the classroom lessons (proxy). Six lessons have no agreement number yet; on those, a native ear decides.
partner_notes.xh: isiXhosa classroom audio is where your corrections matter most: on Funda Wande's classroom recordings the two engines disagree on about a quarter of characters (25.5%, proxy), and on The GGR Lesson 75 of 232 lines split. The meaning check against the partner's own English subtitles still scores 8.5 of 10 (AI-judged).
partner_notes.st: On Funda Wande's Sesotho recordings the two engines agree on 85.9% of characters (proxy), and the meaning check against the partner's own English subtitles scores 9.2 of 10 (AI-judged).
partner_notes.en: On these two English how-tos the engines disagree on 21.5% of characters (proxy): on long natural speech the English engine dropped part of a passage that the second engine caught. Reviewers' corrections will show how often.

meta.title: Speaking review
meta.lead: Help us choose Rumi's voice in each language. Listen to the same sentences read by several voices, say which sounds like a first-language speaker, and tap the words that are said wrong.
meta.dateline: Voices appear as A, B, C… in a different order for every visitor; their names appear after you have rated · every number is labelled measured, proxy or native ear
meta.page_note: Every voice on this page is a candidate. The first native listeners found the voice Rumi ships today understandable, not yet natural; your ratings decide what replaces it.
meta.listen_line: To check what Rumi hears rather than how it sounds, go to the [Listening review](review.html).

howto.heading: How to review
steps: Pick your language and start with the blind comparison: each sentence plays in five or six voices, in an order that is different for everyone, with the names hidden. Listen to all of them.
For each voice, rate two things from 1 to 5: does it sound like a first-language speaker, and is the meaning clear. Tap any word whose pitch or stress is wrong.
Pick the best voice for the sentence, add your name once, and save. Five sentences is the whole job; the voices' names appear once you have saved.
howto.time_note: Five sentences in five or six voices take about ten minutes. You can stop at any sentence; everything you have saved is already counted.

The pitch figure is the first word's pitch against the sentence's own middle, a rough stand-in for what the first native listeners heard at sentence openings; real speakers start high too (25 recordings of first-language speakers reading aloud start a median +3.2 semitones above their own middle), so it is a proxy, not a judgement.
